questions.scenario: A test `assertEquals(new BigDecimal("10.75"), fee)` fails with `expected: <10.75> but was: <10.750>`, although the fee is correct.
questions.question: What is the best fix?
options: Convert both to `double` before comparing
Compare the values, for example `assertThat(fee).isEqualByComparingTo("10.75")`, because `BigDecimal.equals` also compares the scale
Delete the assertion
Use `assertSame`
questions.explanation: 10.75 and 10.750 are equal amounts with different scales. `equals` (and therefore `assertEquals`) treats them as different; `compareTo` and AssertJ's `isEqualByComparingTo` compare the value.

questions.scenario: The fee rule is "₦10 up to and including ₦5,000; ₦25 above". The tests use amounts of ₦100, ₦2,000 and ₦20,000, and all pass, but production charges ₦25 on exactly ₦5,000.
questions.question: Which test cases would have caught it?
options: ₦5,000.00 and ₦5,000.01: exactly on and just above the boundary
A test with a very large amount only
Running the existing tests twice
questions.explanation: A `<` written instead of `<=` only changes behaviour exactly on the boundary. Test just below, on and just above every boundary, ideally in one parameterised test.

questions.scenario: A test class has five copies of the same test method, each with a different amount and expected fee.
questions.question: What is the cleaner way to write it?
options: One `@ParameterizedTest` with a `@CsvSource` row per case
One test with all five assertions and no names
Five separate test classes
A `for` loop inside `main`
questions.explanation: A parameterised test runs each row as its own test with its own name in the report, so a failure tells you exactly which case broke, without duplicated code.

questions.scenario: A wallet must reject an overdraft by throwing `InsufficientFundsException`, and the balance must stay unchanged.
questions.question: Which test checks the rule properly?
options: Call `debit` inside `try`, catch every `Exception`, and do nothing
`assertThatThrownBy(() -> wallet.debit(tooMuch)).isInstanceOf(InsufficientFundsException.class);` followed by an assertion that the balance is unchanged
Assert that the balance is negative after the debit
Only test successful debits
questions.explanation: Check the specific exception type and that no partial change happened. Swallowing every exception would let the test pass even when the wrong thing (or nothing) is thrown.

questions.scenario: `./mvnw test` reports: `Tests run: 12, Failures: 0, Errors: 1` for `WalletTest.creditAddsToBalance`, with a `NullPointerException` at `WalletTest.java:31`.
questions.question: What does "error" (rather than "failure") tell you?
options: An assertion compared two different values
The test threw an unexpected exception before or instead of its assertion; line 31 is where to start, for example a field that was never set up
Maven couldn't find the test
The test was skipped
questions.explanation: A failure means an assertion didn't hold. An error means an exception escaped the test, often missing set-up such as a `@BeforeEach` that wasn't written.

questions.scenario: Two tests pass when run one at a time but one fails when the whole class runs. Both use a `static List<Transfer> transfers` field that the tests add to.
questions.question: What is the problem?
options: JUnit runs tests in parallel by default
Shared static state lets one test's data leak into another; use an instance field (or `@BeforeEach`) so each test starts fresh
The list should be a `LinkedList`
The tests need `@Order` annotations
questions.explanation: JUnit creates a new test-class instance per test, so instance fields are fresh, but a static field is shared. Tests must be independent of each other and of their order.

questions.scenario: A new developer names tests `test1`, `test2` and `testFee`. A CI run fails on `test2`.
questions.question: Why does this matter, and what's better?
options: It doesn't matter; the stack trace is enough
The report doesn't say which rule broke; a name like `rejectsTransfersFromFrozenWallets` reads as the business rule that failed
Test names must start with `test` to run
Long names slow the tests down
questions.explanation: Test names are documentation and the first thing you read in a failure report. JUnit 5 and later don't require a `test` prefix.

questions.scenario: A statement test computes "yesterday" with `LocalDate.now().minusDays(1)` and fails every night between midnight and 1 a.m. on the CI server, which runs in UTC.
questions.question: What principle does it break?
options: Tests must be fast
Tests must be repeatable: the result depends on the real clock and time zone, so inject a fixed `Clock` or pass the date in
Tests must use `@DisplayName`
Tests must not use dates
questions.explanation: Unit tests should give the same result every run. Depending on the current time makes them flaky; topic 7.1 shows how to inject a `Clock`.
